definition: Latent semantic analysis (LSA) is a technique in natural language processing, in particular distributional semantics, of analyzing relationships between a set of documents and the terms they contain by producing a set of concepts related to the documents and terms.
details: LSA assumes that words that are close in meaning will occur in similar pieces of text (the distributional hypothesis). A matrix containing word counts per document (rows represent unique words and columns represent each document) is constructed from a large piece of text and a mathematical technique called singular value decomposition (SVD) is used to reduce the number of rows while preserving the similarity structure among columns. Documents are then compared by cosine similarity between any two columns. Values close to 1 represent very similar documents while values close to 0 represent very dissimilar documents. An information retrieval technique using latent semantic structure was patented in 1988 by Scott Deerwester, Susan Dumais, George Furnas, Richard Harshman, Thomas Landauer, Karen Lochbaum and Lynn Streeter. In the context of its application to information retrieval, it is sometimes called latent semantic indexing (LSI).

explainer.lead: Latent semantic analysis analyses relationships between documents and the terms they contain by producing a set of concepts related to both. It matters as an early method for retrieving by conceptual content rather than mere word matching.

tiers.eli5: Words with similar meanings tend to show up in similar places. By grouping words that keep the same company, you can find documents about the same idea even when they use different words.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers build a word-count-per-document matrix and apply singular value decomposition to reduce rows while preserving similarity among columns. The pitfall is that it works from word counts, not deep context.
tiers.paperLevel: It assumes the distributional hypothesis: words close in meaning occur in similar pieces of text. A matrix of word counts per document is constructed and singular value decomposition reduces the number of rows while preserving the similarity structure among columns; documents are then compared by cosine similarity.

explainer.example: Two documents sharing few exact words can score as similar because their term vectors land close after SVD reduction, measured by cosine similarity.
